speaker: Kathleen Sullivan
title: Supreme Court and Appellate Advocacy | Kathleen Sullivan
question: In legal practice, why does siloing yourself purely as an appellate specialist without trial experience weaken appellate advocacy?
guest: I think it's a mistake to silo yourself as a purely appellate lawyer because, to be a great appellate lawyer, you also have to understand where the record came from and what the trial lawyers did to get it there. And to be part of trials—to be part of, if you're on the plaintiff's side, fashioning complaints, to be part of motion practice, to have helped craft the instructions in a jury trial—is an important part of being a great appellate lawyer, to know how the record goes. To be a great appellate lawyer, you have to know the law, but you have to sometimes know the record better. So I think to focus on facts and have some experience on the trial side as well is a very valuable skill. You can be a great appellate lawyer as your principal focus, but try to get trial experience too.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Appellate advocacy is built entirely on the trial record, and a lawyer who has never made that record tends to misread it. Without trial experience, you lack an instinct for how cases actually unfold: why counsel made a split-second decision not to object, how a judge's evidentiary rulings arise in real time, what a jury likely heard versus what the cold transcript shows, and which errors actually mattered to the outcome. That weakens your judgment on the issues that decide most appeals, namely preservation, standards of review, and harmless error, because those doctrines are rooted in trial-court realities and in deference to the trial judge's vantage point.

It also hurts credibility and issue selection. Appellate judges, many of them former trial judges, are quick to discount arguments that are theoretically elegant but detached from how trials work. A pure specialist may over-value abstract legal error and under-value facts, discretion, and practical consequences.

Finally, trial experience makes you more useful before the appeal: you can advise trial teams on preserving error, framing motions, and building a record, which is often where appeals are won or lost.

models.answer:
Siloing yourself strictly in appellate work detaches legal theory from the practical reality underlying every appeal: how the trial record was actually built. Cold transcripts flatten live courtroom dynamics. An advocate who has never examined witnesses, navigated discovery, or argued mid-trial motions struggles to read between the lines, missing why counsel made tactical trade-offs or why a judge ruled under split-second pressure.

That blind spot distorts issue selection and framing. Because appellate courts apply deferential standards of review and harmless-error doctrines, they reverse only for errors that genuinely prejudiced the outcome. Purely academic specialists often attack technical imperfections that appellate judges recognize as unavoidable or harmless at trial, sacrificing credibility. Lacking courtroom instincts also weakens embedded appellate support and strategic foresight: a lawyer unfamiliar with trial tempo gives impractical error-preservation or jury-instruction advice that alienates judges and juries, and may pursue appellate remedies that prove hollow on remand. Effective appellate advocacy requires understanding how cases are tried, not just how transcripts are read.

noweb.answer: Appellate advocacy reviews the messy, real-time decisions of a courtroom through a cold transcript, and an advocate without trial experience struggles to read what that flat record leaves out. Trial-blind specialists often mistake deliberate tactical trade-offs—like withholding an objection to avoid spotlighting damaging testimony—for blunders, or misjudge how an evidentiary ruling actually affected a jury. That blind spot weakens arguments on prejudice and harmless error, where concrete courtroom dynamics matter far more than doctrinal abstraction. It also breeds tone-deafness under deferential standards like abuse of discretion; appellate judges understand the split-second pressures on trial courts and distrust advocates who demand unrealistic procedural perfection. Moreover, appellate panels care deeply about whether a proposed rule is workable on the ground. Lawyers who have never examined a witness, argued a motion in limine, or settled jury instructions risk urging neat theoretical rules that collapse in practice, and struggle when embedded at trial to preserve issues without alienating the judge or jury.

answers.answer:
Trial experience teaches appellate lawyers how the record is made and what it can support. At trial, lawyers must recognize when to object, make an offer of proof, request an instruction, or seek a ruling. On appeal, those steps can determine whether a court may review an issue, what standard it applies, and whether an error warrants reversal.

Trial experience also helps appellate lawyers assess prejudice. A ruling may look plainly wrong in isolation, but its effect depends on what the jury heard, what other evidence came in, and how the parties tried the case. That judgment helps counsel choose the strongest issues and explain why an error mattered. It also makes appellate counsel more effective before judgment, when there is still time to help the trial team preserve an issue or fill a gap in the record.

Trial experience helps appellate lawyers see how rulings shape the evidence, the arguments counsel can make, and ultimately the verdict. Appeals are generally decided on the trial record, so effective advocacy depends on knowing where an objection or offer of proof matters, whether an issue was preserved, how much deference the trial court receives, and whether an error affected the outcome.

Without that grounding, an appellate lawyer may spot an interesting legal issue but miss a stronger argument supported by the record, or underestimate how hard it will be to show prejudice. Trial experience also improves the advice appellate counsel can give before judgment, when there is still time to preserve an issue and build the record needed to win on appeal.

Trial experience helps appellate lawyers understand how the record was made and what that means for the appeal. A promising argument can fail because counsel raised it too late, failed to make a specific objection, or left excluded evidence out of the record. Time in the trial court gives appellate counsel a better feel for spotting those problems and for working with trial counsel early enough to prevent them.

It also sharpens judgment about which errors are worth pursuing. A lawyer who understands how evidence came in, what the jury heard, and what drove the trial judge’s ruling can make a more persuasive case that an error affected the outcome and that the requested remedy fits. Without that grounding, it’s easier to write a sound argument about the law that gives the appellate court little reason to reverse.
